note: Reel 44: One Word. Draft 3 of the script, approved by the user on 18 Nov ('Yes, approve'). One narrator, the series voice (af_heart, speed 1.0); takes 2-3 run at 0.96 and 1.04. A line that needs a real pause is its own line, so n09/n10, n12/n13 and n21/n22 are split where the script has a full stop and a beat. Numbers are spelled as spoken. The lines ending in b are spare wordings, voiced in the same run in case a contraction that carries the meaning flips (the checklists' lessons from 35, 37 and 38): n03b for 'doesn't stop', n12b for 'doesn't replay', n16b for 'wasn't any', n19b for 'picked a side' (35: 'picked' lost its t), n21b for 'wasn't any'. The approved wording is placed unless the checks mishear it. Facts: docs/research.md.
ref_text: The morning was bright and the street was busy. A cart of fruit stood by the kerb, and the traffic moved past it, slowly at first, then faster.

lines.text: You're the only witness to this crash.
Watch closely.
The driver doesn't stop.
So you're all this man has.
How fast was the rickshaw going when it smashed into the cart?
And the broken glass: left of the cart, or right?
There was no broken glass.
Go back and look.
He never asked if there was any.
He asked where it was.
And some of you could almost see it.
Because your brain doesn't replay a memory.
It rebuilds it, every time, with whatever it's just heard.
Even one word can do it.
In nineteen seventy-four, students whose question said smashed, not hit, were twice as likely, a week later, to remember broken glass.
There wasn't any.
That's why judges usually stop questions like his.
Out here, nobody did.
So if you picked a side, the police are now looking for broken glass.
His glass is fine.
Said there wasn't any? Good.
What hit his windscreen?
The driver keeps going.
Because your brain never replays a memory.
There was none.
So if you chose a side, the police are now looking for broken glass.
Said there was no glass? Good.
